chunks: "An eye mask is a template drawn on the eye diagram, usually a hexagon or rectangle in the centre plus limits above and below, defined by the standard in normalised time and voltage.
A compliant signal's eye has to stay out of it: no signal samples are allowed inside the mask, or only a very small, specified fraction.
The central part guarantees the minimum opening a receiver needs, a minimum eye height and width. The top and bottom limits constrain overshoot and amplitude.
The mask is chosen so that a transmitter or channel that clears it will give a compliant receiver an acceptable bit error rate.
If part of the signal enters the mask, that's a mask violation or 'hit': the signal fails the compliance test, because it doesn't provide enough margin in time or voltage.
Where the hits are tells you why.
Hits at the left and right sides mean too much jitter or too slow an edge, hits at the top and bottom mean ISI or noise closing the eye vertically or too much overshoot.
To fix it, you improve the channel or equalization until it passes, and ideally measure mask margin, the amount you can scale the mask before it gets hit, so you know how comfortably you pass."
